claim: Cognitive function relies on a dynamic, context-sensitive balance between functional integration and segregation in the brain.
source: Cognitive function relies on a dynamic, context-sensitive balance between functional integration and segregation in the brain.
evidence: This is a general statement about cognitive function supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The balance between functional integration and segregation is mediated by global fluctuations in neural gain by projections from ascending neuromodulatory nuclei.
source: Previous work has proposed that this balance is mediated by global fluctuations in neural gain by projections from ascending neuromodulatory nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in the field.

claim: Increases in neural gain directed the network through an abrupt dynamical transition, leading to an integrated network topology that was maximal in frontoparietal 'rich club' regions.
source: We found that increases in neural gain directed the network through an abrupt dynamical transition, leading to an integrated network topology that was maximal in frontoparietal 'rich club' regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling study presented in the manuscript.

claim: The gain-mediated transition was associated with increased topological complexity.
source: This gain-mediated transition was also associated with increased topological complexity, as well as increased variability in time-resolved topological structure, further highlighting the potential computational benefits of the gain-mediated network transition.
evidence: This finding is derived from graph theoretical analyses of the simulated data.

claim: The gain-mediated transition was associated with increased variability in time-resolved topological structure.
source: This gain-mediated transition was also associated with increased topological complexity, as well as increased variability in time-resolved topological structure, further highlighting the potential computational benefits of the gain-mediated network transition.
evidence: This finding is derived from time-resolved analyses of the simulated data.

claim: Neural gain modulation has the computational capacity to mediate the balance between integration and segregation in the brain.
source: These results support the hypothesis that neural gain modulation has the computational capacity to mediate the balance between integration and segregation in the brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The function of complex networks such as the human brain requires a trade-off between functional specialization and global communication.
source: The function of complex networks such as the human brain requires a trade-off between functional specialization and global communication (Deco et al., 2015a; Park and Friston, 2013; Tononi et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The balance between integration and segregation is manifest through dynamically changing patterns of correlated activity, constrained by the brains' structural backbone.
source: Contemporary models of brain function suggest that this balance is manifest through dynamically changing patterns of correlated activity, constrained by the brains' structural backbone (Deco et al., 2013; Honey et al., 2007; Varela et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to contemporary models of brain function.

claim: The extent of integration in the brain is important for effective task performance.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the extent of integration in the brain is important for a range of cognitive functions, including effective task performance (Bassett et al., 2015; Shine et al., 2016a), episodic memory retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017) and conscious awareness (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Godwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent empirical work.

claim: The extent of integration in the brain is important for episodic memory retrieval.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the extent of integration in the brain is important for a range of cognitive functions, including effective task performance (Bassett et al., 2015; Shine et al., 2016a), episodic memory retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017) and conscious awareness (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Godwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Westphal et al., 2017.

claim: The extent of integration in the brain is important for conscious awareness.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the extent of integration in the brain is important for a range of cognitive functions, including effective task performance (Bassett et al., 2015; Shine et al., 2016a), episodic memory retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017) and conscious awareness (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Godwin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barttfeld et al., 2015 and Godwin et al., 2015.

claim: The topological properties of functional brain networks fluctuate over time.
source: Furthermore, the topological properties of functional brain networks have been shown to fluctuate over time (Chang and Glover, 2010; Hutchison et al., 2013), both within individual neuroimaging sessions (Shine et al., 2016a; Zalesky et al., 2014) and over the course of weeks to months (Shine et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: A relatively segregated network architecture is associated with lower metabolic costs.
source: there are also benefits related to a relatively segregated network architecture, including lower metabolic costs (Bullmore and Sporns, 2012; Zalesky et al., 2014) and effective performance as a function of learning (Bassett et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bullmore and Sporns, 2012 and Zalesky et al., 2014.

claim: A relatively segregated network architecture is associated with effective performance as a function of learning.
source: there are also benefits related to a relatively segregated network architecture, including lower metabolic costs (Bullmore and Sporns, 2012; Zalesky et al., 2014) and effective performance as a function of learning (Bassett et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bassett et al., 2015.

claim: The biological mechanisms responsible for driving fluctuations between integration and segregation remain unclear.
source: However, despite these insights, the biological mechanisms responsible for driving fluctuations between integration and segregation remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A candidate mechanism underlying flexible brain network dynamics is the global alteration in neural gain mediated by ascending neuromodulatory nuclei such as the locus coeruleus.
source: A candidate mechanism underlying flexible brain network dynamics is the global alteration in neural gain mediated by ascending neuromodulatory nuclei such as the locus coeruleus (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005 and Sara, 2009.

claim: The locus coeruleus projects diffusely throughout the brain and releases noradrenaline.
source: This small pontine nucleus projects diffusely throughout the brain and releases noradrenaline, a potent modulatory neurotransmitter that alters the precision and responsivity of targeted neurons (Waterhouse et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waterhouse et al., 1988.

claim: Noradrenaline is a potent modulatory neurotransmitter that alters the precision and responsivity of targeted neurons.
source: This small pontine nucleus projects diffusely throughout the brain and releases noradrenaline, a potent modulatory neurotransmitter that alters the precision and responsivity of targeted neurons (Waterhouse et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waterhouse et al., 1988.

claim: There is a nonlinear (inverted-U shaped) relationship between noradrenaline concentration and cognitive performance.
source: Alterations in this system are known to play a crucial role in cognition, as there is evidence for a nonlinear (inverted-U shaped) relationship between noradrenaline concentration and cognitive performance (Robbins and Arnsten, 2009; Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Robbins and Arnsten, 2009 and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The noradrenergic system alters neural gain, increasing the signal to noise ratio of afferent input onto regions targeted by projections from the locus coeruleus.
source: Mechanistically, the noradrenergic system has been shown to alter neural gain (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990) Figure 1b), increasing the signal to noise ratio of afferent input onto regions targeted by projections from the locus coeruleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990 and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Fluctuations in network topology are linked to changes in pupil diameter.
source: Recent work has linked fluctuations in network topology to changes in pupil diameter (Eldar et al., 2013; Shine et al., 2016a; Shine et al., 2018), an indirect measure of locus coeruleus activity (Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014, 2016), providing evidence for a link between the noradrenergic system and network-level topology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Pupil diameter is an indirect measure of locus coeruleus activity.
source: Recent work has linked fluctuations in network topology to changes in pupil diameter (Eldar et al., 2013; Shine et al., 2016a; Shine et al., 2018), an indirect measure of locus coeruleus activity (Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014, 2016), providing evidence for a link between the noradrenergic system and network-level topology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014, 2016.

claim: The mechanisms through which alterations in neural gain mediate fluctuations in global network topology are poorly understood.
source: However, despite these insights, the mechanisms through which alterations in neural gain mediate fluctuations in global network topology are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Biophysical models of large-scale neuronal activity have yielded numerous insights into the dynamics of brain function.
source: Biophysical models of large-scale neuronal activity have yielded numerous insights into the dynamics of brain function, both during the resting state as well as in the context of task-driven brain function (Deco et al., 2009; Honey et al., 2007); for review, see Breakspear, 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work and a review.

claim: Prior research has examined the influence of local dynamics, coupling strength, structural network topology and stochastic fluctuations on functional network topology.
source: Whereas prior research in this area has examined the influence of local dynamics, coupling strength, structural network topology and stochastic fluctuations on functional network topology (Deco et al., 2015b; Deco and Jirsa, 2012; Deco et al., 2017; Gollo et al., 2015; Woolrich and Stephan, 2013), the direct influence of neural gain has not been studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The direct influence of neural gain on functional network topology has not been studied.
source: Whereas prior research in this area has examined the influence of local dynamics, coupling strength, structural network topology and stochastic fluctuations on functional network topology (Deco et al., 2015b; Deco and Jirsa, 2012; Deco et al., 2017; Gollo et al., 2015; Woolrich and Stephan, 2013), the direct influence of neural gain has not been studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: Manipulations of neural gain would modulate the extent of integration in time-averaged patterns of functional connectivity.
source: Based on previous work (Shine et al., 2016a; Shine et al., 2018), we hypothesized that manipulations of neural gain would modulate the extent of integration in time-averaged patterns of functional connectivity.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested, based on previous work.

claim: A generic 2-dimensional neuronal oscillator model was implemented within the Virtual Brain toolbox to generate regional time series constrained by a directed white matter connectome derived from the CoCoMac database.
source: To test this hypothesis, we implemented a generic 2-dimensional neuronal oscillator model (Fitzhugh, 1961; Stefanescu and Jirsa, 2011) within the Virtual Brain toolbox (Jirsa et al., 2010; Sanz Leon et al., 2013) to generate regional time series that were constrained by a directed white matter connectome derived from the CoCoMac database (Kötter, 2004) Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The simulated neuronal time series were passed through a Balloon-Windkessel model to simulate realistic BOLD data.
source: The simulated neuronal time series were passed through a Balloon-Windkessel model to simulate realistic BOLD data.
evidence: This describes a methodological step in the simulation.

claim: Graph theoretical analyses were applied to time-averaged correlations of regional BOLD data to estimate the functional topological signatures of network fluctuations.
source: Graph theoretical analyses were then applied to time-averaged correlations of regional BOLD data to estimate the functional topological signatures of network fluctuations (see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Neural gain (σ) and excitability (γ) were systematically manipulated to simulate the effect of ascending neuromodulatory effects on inter-regional dynamics.
source: To simulate the effect of ascending neuromodulatory effects on inter-regional dynamics, we systematically manipulated neural gain (σ; Figure 1b) and excitability (γ; Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation in the simulation.

claim: Neural gain and excitability alter different aspects of a sigmoidal transfer function, which models the nonlinear relationship between presynaptic afferent inputs and local firing rates.
source: These two parameters alter different aspects of a sigmoidal transfer function, which models the nonlinear relationship between presynaptic afferent inputs and local firing rates (Freeman, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Freeman, 1979.

claim: When the σ and γ parameters are both low, fluctuations in regional activity arise mainly due to noise and local feedback.
source: When the σ and γ parameters are both low, fluctuations in regional activity arise mainly due to noise and local feedback.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: As the σ and γ parameters increase, the influence of activity communicated from connected input regions also increases, leading to non-linear cross-talk and changes in global brain topology and dynamics.
source: As the σ and γ parameters increase, the influence of activity communicated from connected input regions also increases, leading to non-linear cross-talk and hence, changes in global brain topology and dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: Maximal integration occurred at high levels of σ but with intermediate values of γ.
source: We observed a complex relationship between σ, γ and BA, such that maximal integration occurred at high levels of σ but with intermediate values of γ.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: Outside of the zone of maximal integration, the time-averaged connectome was markedly less integrated.
source: Outside of this zone, the time-averaged connectome was markedly less integrated.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: Similar patterns were observed for other topological measures of integration, such as the inverse modularity (Q−1) and global efficiency.
source: Similar patterns were observed for other topological measures of integration, such as the inverse modularity (Q−1) and global efficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Two clear states were observed across the parameter space: one associated with high (ρ ≥0.5) and one with low (ρ <0.5) mean synchrony.
source: Across the parameter space, we observed two clear states (Figure 2b): one associated with high (ρ ≥0.5; yellow) and one with low (ρ <0.5; blue) mean synchrony, with a clear critical boundary demarcating the two states (dotted white line in Figure 2a/b) that was associated with a relative increase in the standard deviation of the order parameter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase synchrony analysis.

claim: A clear critical boundary demarcated the two synchrony states and was associated with a relative increase in the standard deviation of the order parameter.
source: Across the parameter space, we observed two clear states (Figure 2b): one associated with high (ρ ≥0.5; yellow) and one with low (ρ <0.5; blue) mean synchrony, with a clear critical boundary demarcating the two states (dotted white line in Figure 2a/b) that was associated with a relative increase in the standard deviation of the order parameter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase synchrony analysis.

claim: The strong demarcation between states is a known signature of critical behavior.
source: This strong demarcation between states is a known signature of critical behavior (Chialvo, 2010), which can occur at both the regional and network level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chialvo, 2010.

claim: Evidence for both regional and network criticality was observed in the simulation.
source: We observed evidence for both regional and network criticality in our simulation, whereby small changes in parameters (here, σ and γ) facilitated an abrupt transition between qualitatively distinct states.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: At the regional level, a transition from input-driven fluctuations about a stable equilibrium to self-sustained oscillations was observed.
source: At the regional level, this pattern is observed as a transition from input-driven fluctuations about a stable equilibrium to self-sustained oscillations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the regional dynamics analysis.

claim: At the network level, the combined influence of increased gain and structural connections manifest as a transition to high amplitude, inter-regional phase synchrony.
source: At the network level, the combined influence of increased gain and structural connections manifest as a transition to high amplitude, inter-regional phase synchrony (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the network-level dynamics analysis.

claim: Close to the boundary, a truncated Pareto (i.e., power law) scaling regime was observed, spanning up to two orders of magnitude.
source: Close to the boundary, we observed a truncated Pareto (i.e., power law) scaling regime, spanning up to two orders of magnitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluctuation analysis.

claim: The Pareto scaling pattern is consistent with a critical bifurcation within a complex system consisting of many components.
source: This pattern is consistent with a critical bifurcation within a complex system consisting of many components (see Cocchi et al., 2017 and Heitmann and Breakspear, 2017Heitman and Breakspear, 2017 for further discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cocchi et al., 2017 and Heitmann and Breakspear, 2017.

claim: After crossing the boundary, the fluctuation relationship develops a 'knee' above the power-law scaling, consistent with the emergence of a characteristic temporal scale in a super-critical system.
source: After crossing the boundary, this relationship develops a 'knee' above the power-law scaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), consistent with the emergence of a characteristic temporal scale in a super-critical system (Roberts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluctuation analysis, supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2015.

claim: Temporal phase synchrony between regions underlies effective communication between neural regions.
source: A host of contemporary neuroscientific theories hypothesize that temporal phase synchrony between regions underlies effective communication between neural regions (Fries, 2015; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Varela et al., 2001), which would otherwise remain isolated if not brought into temporal lockstep with one another.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical papers.

claim: There was a significant increase in integration (mean BA) in the highly phase synchronous state.
source: By aligning changes in the topological signature of the network to the critical point delineating the two states, we were able to demonstrate a significant increase in integration (mean BA; T798 = 2.57; p=0.01) and decrease in segregation (Q; T798 = −17.44; p<0.001) of network-level BOLD fluctuations in the highly phase synchronous state.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the simulation results.

claim: There was a significant decrease in segregation (Q) in the highly phase synchronous state.
source: By aligning changes in the topological signature of the network to the critical point delineating the two states, we were able to demonstrate a significant increase in integration (mean BA; T798 = 2.57; p=0.01) and decrease in segregation (Q; T798 = −17.44; p<0.001) of network-level BOLD fluctuations in the highly phase synchronous state.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the simulation results.

claim: Global integration demonstrated a sharp increase in the zone associated with the high amplitude synchronous oscillations, particularly for intermediate values of γ.
source: Specifically, global integration demonstrated a sharp increase in the zone associated with the high amplitude synchronous oscillations, particularly for intermediate values of γ (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: The transitions associated with manipulating γ led to an inverse U-shaped relationship: the network was relatively segregated at high and low levels of γ, but integrated at intermediate values of γ.
source: In contrast, the transitions associated with manipulating γ (particularly at high values of σ) led to an inverse U-shaped relationship: the network was relatively segregated at high and low levels of γ, but integrated at intermediate values of γ, albeit with a monotonic relationship when increasing σ for low levels of γ (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: Increases in between-hemisphere connectivity were more pronounced than within-hemisphere connectivity in the ordered state.
source: In addition, increases in between-hemisphere connectivity were more pronounced than within-hemisphere connectivity in the ordered state (within: 0.010 ± 0.017; between: 0.014 ± 0.013; T2,848 = 7.104; p=10−12; see Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the simulation results.

claim: Neural gain and excitability act together to traverse a transition in network dynamics, maximizing inter-regional phase synchrony and integrating the functional connectome.
source: Together, these results suggest that neural gain and excitability act together to traverse a transition in network dynamics, maximizing inter-regional phase synchrony and integrating the functional connectome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Communicability quantifies the number of short paths that can be traversed between two regions of a network.
source: A measure that characterizes the topological balance between integration and segregation is communicability (Estrada and Hatano, 2008), which quantifies the number of short paths that can be traversed between two regions of a network (Mišić et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Estrada and Hatano, 2008 and Mišić et al., 2015.

claim: In networks with high communicability, individual regions are able to interact with a large proportion of the network through relatively short paths, which may facilitate effective communication between otherwise segregated regions.
source: In networks with high communicability, individual regions are able to interact with a large proportion of the network through relatively short paths, which in turn may facilitate effective communication between otherwise segregated regions.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional implications of high communicability.

claim: Communicability was maximal at the critical boundaries between synchronous and asynchronous behavior.
source: In contrast to the relationship observed between neural gain and network integration, communicability was maximal at the critical boundaries between synchronous and asynchronous behavior (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results.

claim: The topological signature of the network was most effectively balanced between integration and segregation as the system transitioned between disorder and order through the modulation of inter-regional synchrony by subtle changes in neural gain.
source: Thus, the topological signature of the network was most effectively balanced between integration and segregation as the system transitioned between disorder and order through the modulation of inter-regional synchrony by subtle changes in neural gain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the communicability results.

claim: The 'resting state' is characterized by significant fluctuations in network topology, in which the brain traverses between states that maximize either integration or segregation.
source: In previous work, we showed that the 'resting state' is characterized by significant fluctuations in network topology, in which the brain traverses between states that maximize either integration or segregation (Shine et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Topological variability was diminished during a cognitively challenging task.
source: This variability was diminished during a cognitively challenging task, and the extent of integration was positively associated with improved task performance (Shine et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The extent of integration was positively associated with improved task performance.
source: This variability was diminished during a cognitively challenging task, and the extent of integration was positively associated with improved task performance (Shine et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The variability of time-resolved integration within each trial was maximized across the critical boundary, as the network switched between disordered and ordered phase synchrony.
source: We found that the variability of time-resolved integration within each trial was maximized across the critical boundary, as the network switched between disordered and ordered phase synchrony (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-resolved analysis.

claim: Changes in neural gain may control the temporal variability of network topology as a function of behavioral state.
source: These results support the hypothesis that changes in neural gain may control the temporal variability of network topology as a function of behavioral state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-resolved variability results.

claim: Rich club regions demonstrated an increase in 'realized' mean gain adjacent to the critical boundary compared to low-degree nodes.
source: Compared to low-degree nodes, rich club regions demonstrated an increase in 'realized' mean gain adjacent to the critical boundary (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from the rich club analysis.

claim: Activity within frontoparietal 'hub' regions was more strongly affected by the interaction between neural gain and network topology than in non-hub regions.
source: In short, this means that activity within frontoparietal 'hub' regions (red in Figure 4a) was more strongly affected by the interaction between neural gain and network topology than in non-hub regions (blue/green in Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rich club analysis results.

claim: The 'realized' gain of individual regions is not simply related to the applied gain but also non-linearly depends on afferent activity from topologically connected regions.
source: Indeed, this result demonstrates that the 'realized' gain of individual regions is not simply related to the applied gain (i.e. input from the ascending noradrenergic system; (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), but also non-linearly depends on afferent activity from topologically connected regions (Figure 4c/d).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the realized gain results.

claim: The observed effect was particularly evident for intermediate values of γ, suggesting that the hub regions were differentially impacted by neural gain at the critical boundary between the asynchronous and synchronous states.
source: The observed effect was particularly evident for intermediate values of γ, suggesting that the hub regions were differentially impacted by neural gain at the critical boundary between the asynchronous and synchronous states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rich club analysis results.

claim: Similar dissociations were observed when comparing regions with high and low diversity.
source: Interestingly, similar dissociations were observed when comparing regions with high and low diversity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting a role for future experiments to disambiguate the importance of degree and diversity in the mediation of global network topology (Bertolero et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the diversity analysis.

claim: 73% of regions were found in both the 'rich' and 'diverse' clubs.
source: However, given the substantial overlap between regions in the 'rich' and diverse' clubs (73% of regions were found in both groups), our results confirm a crucial role for frontoparietal regions in the control of network-level integration as a function of ascending neuromodulatory gain.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the overlap analysis.

claim: Frontoparietal regions play a crucial role in the control of network-level integration as a function of ascending neuromodulatory gain.
source: However, given the substantial overlap between regions in the 'rich' and diverse' clubs (73% of regions were found in both groups), our results confirm a crucial role for frontoparietal regions in the control of network-level integration as a function of ascending neuromodulatory gain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rich club and diversity analyses.

claim: Increasing neural gain transitioned network dynamics across a bifurcation from disordered to ordered phase synchrony with a shift from a segregated to integrated neural architecture.
source: We found that increasing neural gain transitioned network dynamics across a bifurcation from disordered to ordered phase synchrony (Figure 2b) with a shift from a segregated to integrated neural architecture (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the simulation.

claim: The critical boundary between the two synchrony states was associated with maximal communicability and temporal topological variability.
source: The critical boundary between these two states was associated with maximal communicability and temporal topological variability (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the communicability and variability analyses.

claim: The effect of neural gain was felt most prominently in high-degree frontoparietal network hubs.
source: Finally, the effect of neural gain was felt most prominently in high-degree frontoparietal network hubs (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the rich club analysis.

claim: The results confirm the prior hypothesis and complement an emerging view of the brain that highlights a mechanistic bridge between ascending arousal systems and cognition.
source: Together, these results confirm our prior hypothesis and complement an emerging view of the brain that highlights a mechanistic bridge between ascending arousal systems and cognition (Shine et al., 2016a), providing a potential mechanistic explanation for the long-standing notion that noradrenergic activity demonstrates an inverted U-shaped curve with cognitive performance (Robbins and Arnsten, 2009, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall results.

claim: The results provide a potential mechanistic explanation for the long-standing notion that noradrenergic activity demonstrates an inverted U-shaped curve with cognitive performance.
source: Together, these results confirm our prior hypothesis and complement an emerging view of the brain that highlights a mechanistic bridge between ascending arousal systems and cognition (Shine et al., 2016a), providing a potential mechanistic explanation for the long-standing notion that noradrenergic activity demonstrates an inverted U-shaped curve with cognitive performance (Robbins and Arnsten, 2009, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall results.

claim: Network-level fluctuations between segregation and integration in functional (BOLD) networks reflect an underlying transition in synchrony of faster neuronal oscillations.
source: The major result from our study is that network-level fluctuations between segregation and integration in functional (BOLD) networks reflect an underlying transition in synchrony of faster neuronal oscillations, thus providing a previously unknown link between temporal scales in the brain (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is the major conclusion from the study.

claim: At low levels of γ and σ, the governing equations are strongly stable (damped), so that all excursions from equilibrium must be driven by local noise.
source: At low levels of γ and σ, the governing equations are strongly stable (damped), so that all excursions from equilibrium must be driven by local noise – that is, regions are relatively insensitive to incoming inputs (Figure 1b/c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics at low parameter values.

claim: As γ and σ increase, local activity approaches an instability, and consequently incoming activity is able to substantially influence activity in target regions.
source: As γ and σ increase, local activity approaches an instability, and consequently incoming activity is able to substantially influence activity in target regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics as parameters increase.

claim: A stark transition occurs at a critical point in the parameter space, whereby small increases in σ lead to substantial alterations in the phase relationships between regions.
source: A stark transition occurs at a critical point in the parameter space (denoted by the boundary between blue and yellow in Figure 2b), whereby small increases in σ lead to substantial alterations in the phase relationships between regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the phase synchrony analysis.

claim: The network abruptly shifts from stable equilibrium to high-amplitude synchronized oscillation, facilitating an increase in effective communication between otherwise topologically distant regions.
source: Specifically, the network abruptly shifts from stable equilibrium to high-amplitude synchronized oscillation, facilitating an increase in effective communication between otherwise topologically distant regions (Fries, 2005; Varela et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase transition, supported by citations.

claim: The transition point is associated with a peak in informational complexity, suggesting the importance of criticality in maximizing the information processing capacity of global network topology.
source: This same transition point is associated with a peak in informational complexity (Figure 3), further suggesting the importance of criticality in maximizing the information processing capacity of global network topology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the communicability results.

claim: The transition is accompanied by a peak in the topological variability over time: a dynamic instability amongst fast neuronal oscillations yields increased network fluctuations at very slow time scales.
source: Notably, the transition is also accompanied by a peak in the topological variability over time: hence a dynamic instability amongst fast neuronal oscillations yields increased network fluctuations at very slow time scales, again highlighting the crucial role of criticality to multi-scale neural phenomena (Cocchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-resolved variability results, supported by citation.

claim: The recruitment of frontoparietal hub regions at intermediate levels of excitability and neural gain shifts collective network dynamics across a bifurcation, increasing effective interactions between otherwise segregated regions.
source: This suggests that the recruitment of these hub regions at intermediate levels of excitability and neural gain shifts collective network dynamics across a bifurcation, increasing effective interactions between otherwise segregated regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rich club results.

claim: The structural 'rich club' provides topological support to the structural connectome and may facilitate the transition between distinct topological states.
source: This result underlines the effective influence of the structural 'rich club' (Figure 4), which in addition to providing topological support to the structural connectome (van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013), may also facilitate the transition between distinct topological states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rich club results, supported by citation.

claim: This relationship has been demonstrated previously in other studies, either by manipulating the excitability parameter alone or through the alteration of the intrinsic dynamics of the 2d oscillator model.
source: This relationship has been demonstrated previously in other studies, either by manipulating the excitability parameter alone (Deco et al., 2017; Zamora-López et al., 2016), or through the alteration of the intrinsic dynamics of the 2d oscillator model (Curto et al., 2009; Safaai et al., 2015), thus providing a strong conceptual link between structural topology and emergent dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The integrated states facilitated by gain-mediated hub recruitment have been shown to underlie effective cognitive performance, episodic memory retrieval, and conscious awareness.
source: Crucially, the integrated states facilitated by gain-mediated hub recruitment have been shown to underlie effective cognitive performance (Shine et al., 2016a), episodic memory retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017) and conscious awareness (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Godwin et al., 2015), confirming the importance of ascending neuromodulatory systems for a suite of higher-level behavioral capacities.

claim: The findings broadly support the predictions of the neural gain hypothesis of noradrenergic function.

claim: Manipulating neural gain, a plausible instantiation of the effects of ascending noradrenergic tone in the brain, led to marked alterations in network topology.

source: Given the demonstrated links between network topology and cognitive function (Cohen and D'Esposito, 2016; Hearne et al., 2017; Shine et al., 2016a; Shine and Poldrack, 2017), our work thus provides a plausible mechanistic account of the long-standing notion of a nonlinear relationship between catecholamine levels and effective cognitive performance (Robbins and Arnsten, 2009; Shine et al., 2016a; Figure 1a).

source: Combined with our observation of the importance of the interaction between neural gain and high-degree (Figure 4), diverse (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) hub regions, our results thus represent an extension of the neural gain hypothesis that integrates the ascending arousal system with the constraints imposed by multiple order parameters and structural network topology.

claim: Prior computational studies have demonstrated a link between the structural and functional connectome, with the broad repertoire of functional network dynamics bounded by structural constraints imposed by the white-matter backbone of the brain.
source: Prior computational studies have demonstrated a link between the structural and functional connectome, with the broad repertoire of functional network dynamics bounded by structural constraints imposed by the white-matter backbone of the brain (Deco and Jirsa, 2012; Honey et al., 2007, 2009).

claim: The targeted role of gain modulation on local neuronal dynamics have been studied, but the impact of gain on functional network organization has not been pursued.

evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: A putative mechanism has been demonstrated by which a known biological system (the ascending noradrenergic system) can mediate structural-functional changes, by navigating the functional connectome across a topological landscape characterized by alterations in oscillatory synchrony.
source: Here, we have demonstrated a putative mechanism by which a known biological system (namely, the ascending noradrenergic system) can mediate structural-functional changes, essentially by navigating the functional connectome across a topological landscape characterized by alterations in oscillatory synchrony.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall results.

claim: The direct relationship between neural gain manipulation and the ascending noradrenergic system is likely to represent an oversimplification.

claim: Other functional systems, such as the thalamus and fast-spiking interneurons, likely play significant roles in mediating neural gain and the balance between integration and segregation.
source: Indeed, given the complexity and hierarchical organization of the brain, it is almost certain that other functional systems, such as the thalamus (Hwang et al., 2017) and fast-spiking interneurons (Stringer et al., 2016), play significant roles in mediating neural gain and hence, the balance between integration and segregation.
evidence: This is a speculation about other mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The BOLD signal is insensitive to the relative phase of underlying neural dynamics, relating more closely to changes in the local oscillator frequency and fluctuations in the relative amplitude of neural firing.
source: It has been known for some time that the BOLD signal is insensitive to the relative phase of underlying neural dynamics (Foster et al., 2016), relating more closely to changes in the local oscillator frequency and fluctuations in the relative amplitude of neural firing.

claim: Each of the model parameters (gain and coupling) exerts a complex influence on both the oscillator frequencies (and hence, the BOLD activity) and the global synchrony (and hence, the BOLD correlations).
source: Indeed, each of the model parameters used in our experiment (i.e., gain and coupling) exerts a complex influence on both the oscillator frequencies (and hence, the BOLD activity) and the global synchrony (and hence, the BOLD correlations).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Breakspear et al., 2010.

claim: Estimates of connectivity using BOLD time series relate to covariance in amplitude fluctuations among pairs of regions, rather than alterations in phase synchrony.
source: Based on this knowledge, we can infer that estimates of connectivity using BOLD time series relate to covariance in amplitude fluctuations among pairs of regions, rather than alterations in phase synchrony.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between BOLD connectivity and phase synchrony.

source: Our findings thus highlight important constraints on contemporary models of brain function, while also providing crucial implications for understanding effective brain function during task performance or as a function of neurodegenerative or psychiatric disease.
